name: Bến Thành Market
label: Ben Thanh Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Quảng trường Quách Thị Trang' (4 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Công trường Quách Thị Trang' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/39514795: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ben Thanh Market' (221 m across).
notes: Iconic covered market with clock tower.

text.description:
Bến Thành Market is one of the best-known landmarks in central Saigon, and it is easy to see why people photograph it. The entrance block is topped by a three-faced clock tower, with a long, low market hall behind it. It was built in a French Indochinese style, and the roof lines were designed to give shade and natural airflow. The market moved into this building in 1912. It covers about 13,056 square metres and has nearly 1,500 booths, so there is plenty of colour and movement around it.

The classic picture is taken from Quảng trường Quách Thị Trang, the open square opposite the South Gate. From there you look straight at the clock tower, with the main facade spreading out behind it. Guides call this the standard postcard angle, and it gives the clearest view of the tower.

For a busier, more everyday scene, walk round to Phan Bội Châu on the east side. Stalls and street life fill the frame there, and it feels more candid than the formal frontage. Go early if you can, because the facade looks cleaner and there are fewer people crossing your view. The exterior has had a refresh, so it may look different from older travel photos. Traffic is heavy around the square, so take care when stepping back to fit the whole building in.
text.geographic_location: Bến Thành Market stands in Bến Thành Ward, District 1, in the centre of Ho Chi Minh City, at a crossing of four busy streets. The classic viewing area is Quảng trường Quách Thị Trang, the square facing the market's South Gate on the Lê Lợi side.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of District 1 and head for the market's south side, where Quảng trường Quách Thị Trang faces the South Gate. No nearby stops are listed for this spot, so come by taxi or hired scooter and ask to be dropped at the square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) from the square for the clock tower with the facade behind it. If you are close or the square is crowded, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole frontage in. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the clock face and tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Quảng trường Quách Thị Trang (opposite the South Gate, facing the clock tower). The three-faced clock tower above the South Gate, framed by the open square with the market's main facade behind it. For a second, busier view, try Phan Bội Châu on the east side, where stalls and street life fill the scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the clock tower up with the centre column so the facade stays straight. Keep the tower centred and leave some square in the foreground for scale. Wait for a gap in the pedestrians, or let a few people walk through to add life. On Phan Bội Châu, shoot along the row of stalls rather than straight on.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the clock tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out the facade. Hold the phone steady with both hands and keep it level so the vertical lines stay straight. Use night mode in the evening for the lit stalls, and ask vendors before taking close-up photos of them or their goods.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before about 8 AM, when the facade looks cleaner and fewer people are crossing the square. In the evening, the street stalls on Phan Bội Châu and Phan Châu Trinh are lit up and make a lively night scene.

text.access_note: The market is an open, busy shopping area, but check the official site before you go for current opening times, and check on arrival whether the square in front has changed.

name: Landmark 81
label: Landmark 81
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Vinhomes Central Park' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Vinhomes Central Park' (way/375888006): edge nearest the subject (1240 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/622296615: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Vincom Center' (178 m across).
notes: Tallest building in Vietnam, seen across the Saigon River.

text.description:
Landmark 81 is the tallest building in Vietnam, rising 461.2 metres over 81 storeys on the western bank of the Saigon River. Its outline is partly inspired by a bundle of bamboo sticks, a symbol of strength in Vietnamese culture. That slim, stepped shape is why it photographs so well: it makes a clean vertical line against the sky, with the river and open green space around its foot. The tower was finished in April 2018 and stands at the centre of the Vinhomes Central Park development. Its lower floors hold a shopping mall, and an observation deck sits near the top.

The best free view for a full-height shot is the riverside central lawn in Vinhomes Central Park, where the tower rises above the grass, water features and walking paths. Get low and tilt the phone up to make the tower look even taller. Some visitors go up to the upper level of the riverside observation houses in the park for a better frame. The pedestrian bridge inside the park is a second option. If you have time, two other views are worth a look. Bach Dang Wharf Park shows the tower across the river with Thu Thiem 2 Bridge in the same frame. Ong Cay Bridge gives a lit-up foreground at dusk. Early morning is the quietest time in the park, and the light is soft.
text.geographic_location: Landmark 81 is in Thạnh Mỹ Tây ward, on the western bank of the Saigon River, just south of Saigon Bridge. It stands at the heart of the Vinhomes Central Park development, to the north-east of the historic centre.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar stops are listed for this spot. The Vinhomes Central Park area lies north-east of the historic centre, just south of Saigon Bridge on the river's western bank. From there the tower is about 2 minutes on foot to the south-west. The riverside central lawn is the recommended viewing area. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole tower in from the lawn. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched look. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the crown and upper floors.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Vinhomes Central Park (riverside central lawn facing the tower; the pedestrian bridge inside the park is a second option). The tower rising above open lawns, lake or water features and walking paths, with the Saigon River nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Crouch and hold the phone low so the tower stretches upwards, with lawn or water in the foreground. Turn on gridlines and line up the tower with a vertical line so it does not lean. Tilt the phone up as little as you can. If you go to Ong Cay Bridge at dusk, use the lit bridge as a foreground. At Bach Dang Wharf Park, include Thu Thiem 2 Bridge across the river.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the sky stays blue and the top of the tower keeps its detail. At dusk, use night mode and rest your elbows on a railing or your phone against something solid to keep the shot sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, when the park is quiet and the light is soft. Dusk works well at Ong Cay Bridge, where the bridge and nearby towers glow.

text.access_note: The lawns in Vinhomes Central Park are open public space, but check the official site before you go. The tower's observation deck is a separate, ticketed attraction.

name: War Remnants Museum
label: War Remnants Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bảo tàng Chứng tích Chiến tranh' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/186249226: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'War Remnants Museum' (163 m across).
notes: Museum with US military vehicles and aircraft in the courtyard.

text.description:
The War Remnants Museum is one of the most visited museums in Vietnam, and the open-air yard is where most visitors take their photos. Old military hardware stands inside a walled courtyard, with the museum buildings behind. The collection includes a Huey helicopter, an F-5A fighter, an M48 Patton tank and several other aircraft. The aircraft and tank are large, solid shapes that read clearly even on a small phone screen, and the building behind them gives each shot a sense of place.

The building was once the US military's intelligence headquarters. An earlier version of the museum opened in September 1975 under a different name, and it has been called the War Remnants Museum since 1995. The museum counts about half a million visitors a year, roughly two-thirds of them from abroad, so it can get busy.

For the best photos, start in the front courtyard. Equipment is largely not fenced off, so you can walk right up to it. Use the ultra-wide lens for the whole scene, then switch to the default lens (1x) or a little zoom for details such as the rotor, the cockpit or the tank tracks. This is a serious place, so keep your photography respectful. Indoors, flash is not allowed, and the Agent Orange section on the third floor does not allow photos. Skip the most graphic displays out of respect.
text.geographic_location: The museum is at 28 Võ Văn Tần Street in Xuân Hòa ward, Ho Chi Minh City. The courtyard with the aircraft is the first outdoor area you reach.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for 28 Võ Văn Tần Street, Xuân Hòa. Follow the map to the phone icon on the map, which sits at the museum itself. The courtyard is the first area you see on arrival. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit an aircraft and the museum building in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close details such as the helicopter, the tank and the markings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you see the captured US aircraft, including a helicopter, a fighter jet and a tank, with the museum building behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place an aircraft on one side of the frame, with the building filling the background. Move in close with the ultra-wide for a dramatic angle. Step back and use 2x for a calmer, tidier picture. Keep your shots respectful and avoid the most graphic displays indoors.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the aircraft to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks washed out. Switch your flash off, because it is not allowed inside the galleries.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the tour groups arrive, when the light on the aircraft is better. Check the official site for current opening times.

text.access_note: The courtyard can be seen before you buy a ticket, but the indoor galleries are ticketed and have photo restrictions, so check the official site before you go.

name: Independence Palace
label: Independence Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Nguyễn Thị Minh Khai' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of Nguyễn Thị Minh Khai and Nam Kỳ Khởi Nghĩa (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/39598493: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Independence Palace' (135 m across).
notes: Former presidential palace, site of the 1975 end of the war.

text.description:
Independence Palace, also called Reunification Hall, is a historic government building in the middle of Ho Chi Minh City. It was designed by the architect Ngô Viết Thụ. Building began on 1 July 1962 and the hall was inaugurated on 31 October 1966. It is best known as the place where a North Vietnamese tank came through the main gate at 10:45 on 30 April 1975, ending the Vietnam War. Today it is a museum and a hall for state events.

For a phone photo, the best-known view is the full front, but the corner on Nguyễn Thị Minh Khai gives you something different. A small octagonal pavilion with a curved tile roof sits on a raised mound, with the palace's green lawns behind it. It is usually quieter than the front, and the pavilion gives the picture a human scale that a plain shot of the building lacks.

If you also want the classic front view, with the replica tank at the entrance and the symmetrical wings and flags, go to the Nam Kỳ Khởi Nghĩa side. For a calmer view of the back of the building framed by trees and lawn, try Huyền Trân Công Chúa.
text.geographic_location: Independence Palace stands in central Ho Chi Minh City, in a large garden.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the central area of Ho Chi Minh City and go by taxi or hired scooter to the corner of Nguyễn Thị Minh Khai at the northwest corner of the palace grounds. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the pavilion, the lawns and the palace in one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier picture of the pavilion with the palace behind it. Use the telephoto (2x or more) to pick out the palace details from a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Nguyễn Thị Minh Khai and Nam Kỳ Khởi Nghĩa (left (northwest) corner of the grounds, next to the octagonal pavilion on its mound). The small octagonal pavilion with its curved tile roof sitting on a raised mound, with the palace's green lawns behind it. From here the palace building lies to the south.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the pavilion in the foreground, slightly off-centre, and let the lawns lead the eye back to the palace. Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level so the building does not look tilted. If you want the full front view instead, go to the Nam Kỳ Khởi Nghĩa side. For the back of the palace with trees and open lawn, try Huyền Trân Công Chúa.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pavilion roof or the palace to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the building keeps its detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. Midday sun can be harsh on the pale walls.

text.access_note: The palace grounds and interior are a ticketed visit, and viewing points inside the grounds may need a ticket, so check the official site before you go for tickets and opening times.

name: Nguyễn Huệ Boulevard
label: Nguyen Hue Walking St
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Nguyễn Huệ' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Nguyễn Huệ' (way/341504312): point nearest the subject (657 m long).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q11300021: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Pedestrian boulevard leading to City Hall.

text.description:
Nguyễn Huệ Boulevard is the wide, car-free street that runs through the middle of District 1, from the front of the City Hall down to the Saigon River. It began as a canal, which was filled in during 1886–1887 and became a boulevard. It was turned into a pedestrian street in 2015, and at Tết (lunar new year) it becomes the Nguyễn Huệ Flower Street. That mix of wide open space and old and new buildings gives you plenty to frame.

The classic photo is taken from the north end, in front of the People's Committee Building, at the Ho Chi Minh statue. The bronze statue and flowerbeds fill the foreground, and the yellow, French-style City Hall rises behind them. Guides call this the postcard angle on the street, and it is easy to frame even if you only have a minute. One guide suggests crouching at the edge of the flowerbed so the clock tower fits in.

Two other views are worth a short walk. The multi-level Café Apartments facade at 42 Nguyễn Huệ is the boulevard's most recognisable building. At the river end, Bach Dang Wharf Park looks across the water to the skyline and the Bitexco Financial Tower.

The statue area is often crowded, especially at weekends and on holidays, so take a few frames quickly and be patient. Flower displays and fountains change, so expect the scene to look a little different from older photos.
text.geographic_location: In District 1, in the centre of Ho Chi Minh City. The boulevard runs from the Ho Chi Minh City Hall end at Lê Thánh Tôn Street down to the Saigon River waterfront on Tôn Đức Thắng Boulevard.
text.directions_text: The nearest station is Opera House station on Ho Chi Minh City Metro Line 1, which has many exits onto the boulevard. From there, walk along Nguyễn Huệ towards the City Hall end at Lê Thánh Tôn Street, where the Ho Chi Minh statue stands. If you are coming from elsewhere in the city, a taxi to the City Hall end is simplest. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the statue, flowerbeds and City Hall together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the square is busy and you want to take in the whole front of the building. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the clock tower or architectural details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Nguyễn Huệ (north end, in front of the Ho Chi Minh City People's Committee Building, at the Ho Chi Minh statue). The boulevard's northern end, with the bronze Ho Chi Minh statue and flowerbeds in the foreground and the yellow colonial City Hall behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the statue slightly off-centre, with the City Hall filling the space behind. For a lower angle, crouch at the edge of the flowerbed with the phone held low, so the clock tower fits above the statue. For a second view, walk down to 42 Nguyễn Huệ for the Café Apartments facade, or to Bach Dang Wharf Park for the river and the Bitexco Financial Tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the City Hall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky stays blue and the yellow walls keep their colour. Wait a moment for people to move out of the frame. Use night mode after dark and hold the phone steady against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Weekend evenings are lively because the whole boulevard is closed to vehicles, but the statue area is crowded then. For clearer views of the statue and City Hall, try early in the day on a weekday. At Tết the street is decorated as the Flower Street, so expect a very different scene.

text.access_note: Nguyễn Huệ is an open, pedestrian-only public street with free access to the viewpoint, but check current conditions such as events and flower displays before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early in the day on a weekday is likely to be quieter at the statue.
The City Hall and boulevard are lit up after dark, so night mode can help.
Crouching at the flowerbed edge helps include the clock tower in the photo.

name: Hotel Majestic (Saigon)
label: Majestic Hotel
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Đồng Khởi – Tôn Đức Thắng corner' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Đồng Khởi Street and Tôn Đức Thắng Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/193142038: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Majestic Hotel' (131 m across).
notes: Art deco riverside hotel from 1925.

text.description:
The Majestic is one of the best-known old buildings on the Saigon riverfront. It stands on the corner where Đồng Khởi Street (the old Rue Catinat) meets the riverside quay, and it is a good first stop for a colonial-style street shot. It was first built in 1925 as a three-storey French colonial hotel with 44 bedrooms, with some Art Deco and classical French Riviera influence. It has been changed and enlarged several times since, including a Neo-Renaissance-style renovation in 1994, and it is now a five-star hotel owned by Saigontourist Group. The building has a long and sometimes turbulent history, which adds to the interest of the frontage.

From here the hotel is seen head-on, with the river side of the building visible beside it. Because you are close, the building fills the frame quickly, so the ultra-wide lens helps. Look for the long horizontal lines of the facade and keep them level with the gridlines. A second option is Bến Bạch Đằng, the riverbank promenade, where you can frame the river-facing side with the Saigon River in front. The river road is busy with heavy traffic and noise, so wait for a gap before stepping back, and keep clear of the kerb.
text.geographic_location: The hotel is in District 1, in the centre of Ho Chi Minh City, on the bank of the Saigon River at the corner of Đồng Khởi and Tôn Đức Thắng. It faces the Bạch Đằng riverside quay.
text.directions_text: Start from the city centre in District 1 and go by taxi or hired scooter to the corner of Đồng Khởi and Tôn Đức Thắng, beside the river. Once you are the hotel building lies to the west and is about 1 minute on foot away. The riverside promenade is a short walk along the quay. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full frontage from the corner. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Đồng Khởi Street and Tôn Đức Thắng Street (junction facing the river, in front of the hotel's main frontage). The colonial-style hotel frontage seen head-on from the street junction, with the river side of the building visible beside it. This gives the classic full-building view, with the river side of the building visible beside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the vertical edges of the building with them, so the facade does not lean. Hold the phone level and at chest height. Keep the sky and the full roofline in the frame. For a second shot, walk to Bến Bạch Đằng and frame the river-facing side with the Saigon River in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright. Take a few shots, because traffic will pass through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows. Night mode can work after dark if you hold the phone steady against something solid.

text.access_note: The exterior is easy to photograph from the public street and riverside, but the hotel itself is a private business, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: Saigon Central Post Office
label: Central Post Office
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Công xã Paris' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Công trường Công xã Paris' (way/803199399): middle (256 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/39514793: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Saigon Central Post Office' (114 m across).
notes: Gustave Eiffel-era yellow colonial building with arched hall.

text.description: The Saigon Central Post Office is a working post office with a pale yellow front, arched windows and a big central clock. It sits in Paris Commune Square, right beside Saigon Notre-Dame Basilica, so the two buildings share one open square and one photo stop. It was built between 1886 and 1891, when Vietnam was part of French Indochina, and mixes Gothic, Renaissance and French influences. It was designed by Alfred Foulhoux. It is often wrongly credited to Gustave Eiffel, which is a good fact to share with your photo. Look along the outside wall for small plaques honouring scientists such as Morse, Ampere, Volta, Ohm and Faraday. Inside are two painted maps from 1892, one of telegraph lines in southern Vietnam and Cambodia and one of Saigon and its surroundings. The building photographs well because the facade is wide, symmetrical and clearly lit, and the square gives you room to step back. Start across the square from the front. From there the whole facade fits in one frame, with the cathedral side of the square beside it. Early in the day the light falls on the facade from the left, which gives it a warmer look. The area right in front of the entrance can be busy with tour groups, so take your wide shot first and move closer afterwards. Photography inside the main hall is allowed.
text.geographic_location: In Saigon ward, in the centre of Ho Chi Minh City, on Paris Commune Square (Công xã Paris). It stands directly next to Saigon Notre-Dame Basilica, the city's cathedral.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so go by taxi or hired scooter to Saigon Notre-Dame Basilica in Saigon ward. The post office is the yellow building right next to it, on Paris Commune Square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) from across the square for the full facade. If you are stuck close to the building, the ultra-wide (0.5x) will fit it all in but will make the edges lean, so use it sparingly. Try telephoto (2x or more) for the clock and the arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Công xã Paris (across the square from the facade, toward the cathedral side). The full yellow front of the post office with its central clock and arched windows, framed by the square and the cathedral next door. Stepping back to the far side of the square gives a wider frame with less distortion.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the clock and let the arched windows run evenly to each side. Turn on gridlines and line them up with the building's edges so the walls stay upright. For a different shot, walk closer on Công xã Paris for a straight-on view of the entrance arch and clock, with the decoration filling the frame. Inside, the main hall's long vaulted ceiling leads the eye down the central aisle toward the portrait of Ho Chi Minh at the far end.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the yellow walls. In the dimmer main hall, hold the phone steady and try night mode.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Before 9am, when the facade looks warmer and the light falls on it from the left (per one guide). It is also likely to be quieter then.

text.access_note: The square is open to pedestrians, but the post office is a working building, so check the official site before you go for opening times and any rules inside.

name: Ho Chi Minh City Opera House
label: Saigon Opera House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Đồng Khởi' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Đồng Khởi nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/801710792: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Saigon Opera House' (94 m across).
notes: Elegant 1900 colonial theatre on Lam Sơn Square.

text.description:
The Ho Chi Minh City Opera House (Nhà hát Thành phố) is a French colonial theatre in the middle of downtown Saigon. It was designed by French architects, with Félix Olivier credited for its particular character. It was finished by 1 January 1900. The façade is ornate and shaped like the Petit Palais in France, built the same year. Arched windows, carved reliefs and a grand central entrance make it easy to frame, and the building stands clear of its surroundings. Some of the original decoration was taken off in 1943 and part of it was put back when the façade was restored in 1998. Today the theatre seats 500, though it once held up to 1,800.

The most recommended photo looks west down Đồng Khởi street towards the front of the building. This gives a street-level view with the façade at the end of the road, and it is quietest early in the morning. The Đồng Khởi viewpoint is in the middle of the road, which is risky, so use it only when traffic is completely clear and otherwise stay on the pavement. If you want the whole front framed symmetrically, Công Trường Lam Sơn is a good alternative. In some frames from there, the Continental and Rex hotels appear on either side. For something closer, the entrance steps and balustrades make a good backdrop for portraits. This is a busy junction full of motorbikes, so take your photos from the pavement and not from the road.
text.geographic_location: The Opera House is in the heart of downtown Ho Chi Minh City, near Đồng Khởi street. It sits close to Công Trường Lam Sơn (Lam Sơn Square) and the Continental and Rex hotels.
text.directions_text: From the Đồng Khởi and Nguyễn Du area of downtown Saigon, the Opera House is easy to spot. If you are coming from elsewhere in the city, Ho Chi Minh City Metro Line 1 has an Opera House Station. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the street view down Đồng Khởi with the façade at the end. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and cannot fit the whole front in. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the reliefs, balustrades and window details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Đồng Khởi (middle of the road, looking west toward the building; use only when traffic is clear). A street-level perspective down Dong Khoi toward the opera house facade. Keep to the pavement. For a closer view of the entrance steps and ornamentation, walk up to the front of the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the entrance on the central vertical line so the façade looks balanced. A street-level view with the road leading to the building works well. As an alternative, Công Trường Lam Sơn gives a symmetrical full-front view. For portraits, use the steps and balustrades with the building behind and try portrait mode.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the façade to set focus, then pull the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Check the edges of the frame for passing motorbikes before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around 7:30 AM, when the road is clear of heavy traffic.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from the surrounding pavements, but the interior is only open with a show ticket and photography is not allowed during performances, so check the official site before you go.

name: Hotel Continental Saigon
label: Continental Hotel
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Quảng trường Lam Sơn' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Công trường Lam Sơn' (roads).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q5911405: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Historic 1880 colonial hotel on Đồng Khởi Street.

text.description:
The Continental is a colonial-era hotel on the corner of Đồng Khởi Street and Lam Sơn Square, right beside the Saigon Municipal Theatre (the Opera House). It was built in 1878, opened in 1880 and is generally described as the oldest hotel in Vietnam. It was named after the Hôtel Continental in Paris. For a phone photo, its appeal is the pairing of two landmarks. From the square you can fit the hotel's colonial corner and the Opera House alongside it into one frame, with open space in front, so you don't have to shoot upwards from a crowded pavement.

The hotel has a long story. During the First Indochina War it was nicknamed Radio Catinat, because journalists and politicians met there. Graham Greene stayed here, and the hotel appears in his novel The Quiet American. It also appears in the 1992 film Indochine. Mentioning this to the people you're travelling with gives the picture some context.

Stand on Quảng trường Lam Sơn and shoot back across the square towards the corner. If you want a second angle, walk to Đồng Khởi Street and photograph the facade and balconies along the street, with the corner and square at the edge of the frame. Keep your phone level so the vertical lines of the building don't lean. Traffic and pedestrians are likely to cross your frame, so take a few shots and pick the cleanest. The courtyard, staircase and lobby are inside the hotel and are not part of this outdoor photo spot.
text.geographic_location: In Saigon, the central ward of Ho Chi Minh City, on the corner of Đồng Khởi Street and Lam Sơn Square. It stands next to the Saigon Municipal Theatre (the Opera House).
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar stop is listed for this spot, so start from the central Saigon area around Đồng Khởi Street and Lam Sơn Square, by taxi or hired scooter. The hotel stands on the corner of the square, next to the Opera House. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the hotel corner and the Opera House together. If you cannot fit both in, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use 2x or more on the telephoto lens for details such as balconies and windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Quảng trường Lam Sơn (across the square from the hotel's corner with Đồng Khởi, beside the Opera House). The hotel's colonial facade on the corner, with the Saigon Opera House alongside it across the open square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the hotel corner on one of the vertical lines, with the Opera House filling the other side of the frame. Keep the phone level so the walls stay straight. As an alternative, walk to Đồng Khởi Street and photograph the facade and balconies along the street, with the corner and square at the edge of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the hotel facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the building keeps its colour and detail. Take a few shots in a row, since people and vehicles pass through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is likely to give softer light and fewer people in the square. Check the light on the day, as the facade can be in shade or glare depending on the hour.

text.access_note: The square and the street frontage are public places; the hotel itself is a working hotel, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: Bitexco Financial Tower
label: Bitexco Tower
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/804073951: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Bitexco Financial Tower' (110 m across).
notes: Lotus-bud skyscraper with a Skydeck viewing platform.

text.description: Bitexco Financial Tower is a 68-floor glass skyscraper in Saigon's Financial District, the second tallest building in Ho Chi Minh City. It is 262.5 metres tall. When it was completed in 2010 it was the tallest building in Vietnam. The architect, Carlos Zapata, took the lotus, Vietnam's national flower, as his inspiration, and you can see it in the tapering, petal-like sweep of the glass. Around 6,000 individually cut glass panels make up the surface, which is why it catches so much sky and so many reflections. The most photogenic detail is the helipad, which juts out from the 52nd floor on the southern side and looks like a lotus bud. For a phone photo, treat the tower as a tall, simple shape. Keep the camera as upright as you can, switch on gridlines and line the edges of the tower up with the vertical lines so it doesn't lean. Use the phone icon on the map for the big, close-up view looking up. If you want the whole tower in one frame, walk back until the top fits. Adding something in the foreground, such as trees, a lamp or people crossing, gives the picture scale. Look at the helipad and the crown separately, as they make good detail shots on their own. There is also an observation deck on the 49th floor, so you can photograph the city from the tower as well as the tower itself.
text.geographic_location: Bitexco Financial Tower stands in the Financial District of District 1, in central Ho Chi Minh City, next to the city's state treasury and close to Nguyễn Huệ Boulevard.
text.directions_text: Head to the Financial District or Nguyễn Huệ Boulevard in District 1 and walk from there to the tower. Once you are close, walk to the phone icon on the map at the foot of the tower. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are at the foot of the tower and want to take in its full height. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view from further back. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the helipad and the crown.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Tilt the phone up and use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for a dramatic look-up shot, then walk a little way back from the base for a view of the whole tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower's edges up with the vertical lines. Hold the phone level, then tilt it only slightly upwards, as a steep tilt makes the tower lean. Include a tree or a lamp at the edge of the frame for scale. For a detail shot, zoom in on the helipad on the southern side.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the glass to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky doesn't wash out the glass. In the evening, hold the phone steady against a wall or railing and let night mode do its work.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon to dusk is a good choice, when the glass picks up warm colour and the city lights start to come on. Midday sun can make the glass look flat and bright.

text.access_note: The area around the tower is a public city space, but the observation deck and other parts of the building may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.

name: Notre-Dame Cathedral Basilica of Saigon
label: Notre-Dame Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Công trường Công xã Paris' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Công trường Công xã Paris' (way/803199399): middle (256 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/801950766: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Saigon Notre Dame Cathedral' (105 m across).
notes: Red-brick French colonial cathedral from the 1880s.

text.description:
Built of bright red brick with two tall bell towers, this is the cathedral most visitors want in their Ho Chi Minh City photos. The walls went up between 1877 and 1880, and the bricks came from Toulouse in France. They have kept their colour remarkably well, which is why the facade glows in good light. The two towers were added in 1895 and are about 58 metres tall. In front stands the white statue of Our Lady of Peace, installed in 1959, and the cathedral has been called Notre-Dame since then.

The best-known frame is from the square in front of the facade, with the white statue in the foreground and both towers behind it. One frame holds all three, and the white figure stands out well against the red brick. Guides say the early morning or late afternoon light is warmest on the brick.

The cathedral is being restored, and completion is expected around 2027. Scaffolding may partly cover the front, so check on the day how much it spoils the view. If the facade is covered, try a tighter shot of the statue with one tower, or the other viewpoints below. The Saigon Central Post Office across the square lets you frame the cathedral through its yellow arches. Diamond Plaza gives a raised view of the cathedral and the roundabout below.
text.geographic_location: In the Saigon ward of central Ho Chi Minh City, in the square in front of the cathedral. The Saigon Central Post Office stands on the opposite side of the square.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Saigon ward area in the city centre and go by taxi or hired scooter, asking for Notre-Dame Cathedral. Get out near the square in front of the cathedral. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) so the statue and both towers fit in one frame from the square. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer view with less stretching at the edges. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the statue's face, the brickwork or the tops of the towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Công trường Công xã Paris (Stand in the square in front of the facade, with the statue of Our Lady of Peace in the foreground). The full red-brick facade with both bell towers, framed by the white Virgin Mary statue in the garden. The cathedral is to the west of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the statue up with the gap between the two towers for a balanced, symmetrical shot. Hold the phone upright, not tilted back, or the towers will lean inwards. If the facade is under scaffolding, crop in on the statue and one tower. For a different view, shoot the cathedral through the yellow arches of the Saigon Central Post Office, or look down on it and the roundabout from Diamond Plaza.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the red brick to set focus and exposure, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is washing out. Use portrait mode only for a close shot of the statue, and check that the edges of the towers stay sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is warm on the red brick.

text.access_note: The square and the outside of the cathedral can be photographed from outside, but the interior is closed to tourists except at Mass times, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: An ultra-wide lens helps fit the statue and both towers into one frame when standing close to the facade.
Tilting a phone upwards makes tall buildings appear to lean inwards.
Dragging the exposure slider down can stop a bright sky washing out in a photo.

name: Jade Emperor Pagoda
label: Jade Emperor Pagoda
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Chùa Ngọc Hoàng' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1272651080: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Jade Emperor Pagoda' (37 m across).
notes: Atmospheric Taoist temple with incense coils and carved deities.

text.description:
The Jade Emperor Pagoda is a working temple in District 1, and its coral-pink walls, roof decorations and carved details make it an easy place to photograph. It mixes Taoist, Buddhist and Confucian traditions. It is also known as Chùa Ngọc Hoàng, and since 1984 by the Buddhist name Phước Hải Tự, which means "Luck Sea Temple". It was founded by Liu Daoyuan, a Cantonese merchant who had migrated to the city. Barack Obama visited it during his state trip to Vietnam on 22 May 2016.

The best pictures come from the open front yard and courtyard, looking towards the main hall. From here you can take in the colour of the exterior, the roof decorations and the carving without going inside. Photography inside the halls is restricted or unclear, so check on the day, treat the courtyard as your main spot and follow any signs you see. Keep flash off and ask before photographing anyone who is praying. Do not photograph people at the fertility shrine. The entrance is shaded by trees and hard to spot from the street, so allow a few minutes to find it. Expect it to be very busy during Tet and on the 9th day of the first lunar month.
text.geographic_location: The pagoda is in District 1, Ho Chi Minh City. The entrance is shaded by trees and hard to spot from the street.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot. Head for District 1 by taxi or hired scooter and ask to be dropped at Chùa Ngọc Hoàng (Jade Emperor Pagoda). The entrance is shaded by trees and easy to miss from the street, so allow time to find the shaded entrance. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the front of the main hall. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the courtyard is too tight to fit the whole building in. Use telephoto (2x-5x) for roof decorations and carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. You are at the Jade Emperor Pagoda itself. From here you can photograph the coral-pink exterior, the roof decorations and the carved details without going inside.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the main hall so its roofline sits level along a grid line. Take one wide shot of the whole frontage, then step closer or zoom for the carving and roof details. Keep people who are praying out of the frame, or ask first.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Switch flash off. Tap on the pink wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the bright sky is washing out the roof decorations.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon gives warm light on the exterior. Early morning is quieter and has fewer crowds.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship, so dress respectfully and follow the signs; admission is free, but check the official site before you go for current opening hours and photography rules.

name: Saigon Zoo and Botanical Gardens
label: Saigon Zoo & Gardens
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cổng chính Thảo Cầm Viên' (4 web pages); placed at crossing of Nguyễn Bỉnh Khiêm and Lê Duẩn (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/32735038: large area 'Saigon Zoo and Botanical Gardens' (855 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Historic 1869 zoo and park near the Citadel site.

text.description: Saigon Zoo and Botanical Gardens, known locally as Sở Thú, is the oldest zoo and botanical garden in Vietnam. Admiral Pierre-Paul de La Grandière commissioned it in 1864 and it opened to the public in 1869, so it is one of the oldest continuously operating zoos in the world. For a phone photographer the easiest and most recognisable picture is the main entrance: a red-roofed, arched gate with its signage, and big leafy trees rising behind it. That frame says 'zoo and gardens' at a glance, and it is a good opening shot for a visit. The grounds are large, with roughly 590 animals of 125 species and about 1,830 trees and plants of 260 species, some of them over 100 years old. Inside there is also the Ho Chi Minh City Museum of History and a temple to the Hùng Kings, which began life as a memorial to soldiers. Shoot the gate from the street at the corner, so the arch, the sign and the tree canopy all sit in one frame. Wait a moment for people to move out of the way, or include a few of them to show the scale of the gate. Once inside, flash is discouraged near the animals, so rely on your phone's normal daylight settings. Entry may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In District 1 of Ho Chi Minh City, at the north-east end of Lê Duẩn Boulevard and along Nguyễn Bỉnh Khiêm Street, beside the Thị Nghè Canal. The main gate sits at a street corner.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground or tram stop to give you, so head for the north-east end of Lê Duẩn Boulevard in central District 1 by taxi or hired scooter. Ask for the main gate, Cổng chính Thảo Cầm Viên. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the gate and want the arch, the signage and the tree canopy all in one frame. The default lens (1x) gives a more natural look with less edge stretching if you can step back across the street. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the roof and signage.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Nguyễn Bỉnh Khiêm and Lê Duẩn (main entrance gate, at the corner of the two streets). The red-roofed, arched main gate with its signage and large leafy trees behind it, framed from the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the gate on the central vertical line so the arch looks symmetrical. Keep the phone level, so the roofline does not tilt, and leave some sky and treetop above the roof. If you want a different view, one guide suggests a wide shot from the main entrance's sweeping staircase.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the gate to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the bright sky is washing out the red roof. Keep the flash off, especially once you are near the animals.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is the best choice, when the light is softer and the grounds are quieter.

text.access_note: The gate view is from the street, but entry to the zoo and gardens is likely to be ticketed and has set hours, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning light at the gate is softer and the area is quieter.
Flash photography is discouraged near the animals.
The main gate is the easiest entrance to find.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep a bright sky from washing out the red roof.
The walk from the stand-here point to the subject point takes roughly 1–2 minutes.

name: Tân Định Church
label: Tan Dinh Church
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hai Bà Trưng' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of Hai Bà Trưng and Đinh Công Tráng (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/60118189: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Tân Định Church' (68 m across).
notes: Famous pink Romanesque-Gothic church.

text.description: Tân Định Church is known locally as the pink church, and the colour is the reason to come. The whole building, outside and in, has been painted pastel pink since 1957, and against a blue sky or the greenery of the street it stands out well. Its formal name is the Church of the Sacred Heart of Jesus. It was completed on 16 December 1876, in the French colonial period, and the style is mainly neo-Romanesque with some neo-Gothic and neo-Renaissance touches. It is the second-largest church in Ho Chi Minh City, after Notre-Dame Basilica. The tall bell tower and the arched details give you plenty to work with. The classic photo is taken from the pavement on Hai Bà Trưng, opposite the church, where you can fit the full facade and the tower in one frame. A low angle makes the tower look taller, and you can add a friend in the foreground for scale. If you want a closer, more graphic picture, go to the white arched gate and frame the pink facade through the arch. Hai Bà Trưng is a busy road, so keep to the pavement and watch the traffic while you compose. Visiting hours seem to vary, and the interior is for worshippers during mass, so check opening times locally before you go. One guide also mentions possible restoration work on the outside walls, which could affect the view.
text.geographic_location: Tân Định Church stands at 289 Hai Bà Trưng Street in District 3 of Ho Chi Minh City; the parish shares its name with District 1's Tân Định ward. The photo viewpoint is on the opposite side of the street from the church.
text.directions_text: No station is listed close by, so head for Hai Bà Trưng Street in District 3, near the church at no. 289, by taxi or hired scooter, and ask for Nhà thờ Tân Định. Get out on the side of the street opposite the church, where Cộng Cà Phê is. From there the church is across the road to the south, and walking up to its gate takes about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from across the road to get the whole facade and tower. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is crowded or you are close to the gate and cannot fit the tower in. Try 2x or 3x for details such as the tower top and the arches.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Hai Bà Trưng and Đinh Công Tráng (opposite the church, on the side where Cộng Cà Phê stands). The full pink facade and bell tower framed against the sky, shot from ground level across the busy road.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the tower upright on one of the vertical lines. Crouch a little and tilt the phone up for a low angle that makes the spire look taller. Leave a bit of sky above the tower. If you want a person in the picture, have them stand to one side of the frame. As an alternative, the café's upper level gives a higher, eye-level view of the whole facade, and the white arched gate gives a close view of the pink wall through the arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pink wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky stays blue and the pink does not wash out. Use portrait mode only for the person, not for the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the facade glows. One guide suggests about 3:00 to 4:30 pm.

text.access_note: The church is a working place of worship, and the interior is reportedly open only to worshippers during mass, with the gate closing around lunchtime and opening days varying, so check opening times locally before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Ultra-wide shots taken close to a building can make the edges look stretched.
Standing a little back and zooming to 2x or 3x gives a more natural perspective on the tower than going closer.
Tilting the phone upwards makes vertical lines lean inwards slightly.

name: Ho Chi Minh City Hall
label: People's Committee Hal
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Nguyễn Huệ Walking Street' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Nguyễn Huệ Walking Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/341504305: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Ho Chi Minh City Hall' (218 m across).
notes: French colonial Hôtel de Ville, lit up at night, with the Ho Chi Minh statue in front.

text.description:
Ho Chi Minh City Hall is the grand yellow-and-white building at the head of Nguyễn Huệ Boulevard. It is still the working home of the city's People's Committee and People's Council. The French began building it in 1898 and it opened in 1909 after about eleven years of work. The architect was Fernand Gardè, who took ideas from the town hall in Paris and from the bell towers of northern France. That gives it a tall central clock tower, two smaller towers either side and long, matching wings. Look closely at the front and you will see wreaths, columns and three sculptures of Marianne under the pediments. A second storey was added to the wings in the 1940s.

It photographs well because the boulevard leads straight to it, so the whole front is symmetrical. The popular picture is taken from the centre line of the street, with the bronze Ho Chi Minh statue in the foreground and the clock tower behind. If the building will not fit, step back along the street. Try it in late afternoon, when the light on the facade is softer, and again in the evening once the building is lit. The area is decorated with flowers seasonally, around the Tết festival, which adds colour. For a different view, a low, upward-angled shot of the statue from Hồ Chí Minh Square, with the clock tower rising behind it, also works well. Keep your phone level so the tower does not lean.
text.geographic_location: It stands in downtown Ho Chi Minh City's Saigon ward, at the north-west end of Nguyễn Huệ Boulevard. It sits between Pasteur, Lý Tự Trọng, Đồng Khởi and Lê Thánh Tôn streets.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so navigate to the Nguyễn Huệ Boulevard area in central Saigon. Once you are on the boulevard, walk along its centre line towards the north-west end, where the City Hall closes the view. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full facade, clock tower and statue together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and cannot fit the building in. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the clock tower and the Marianne sculptures.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Nguyễn Huệ Walking Street (central axis of the pedestrian boulevard, toward the north-west end at the City Hall). The full yellow-white facade and clock tower of the City Hall at the far end of the boulevard, with the bronze Ho Chi Minh statue placed in the foreground. The full-facade view, with the yellow-white front and clock tower behind the bronze Ho Chi Minh statue in the foreground, is taken from farther back along the boulevard centre line. Standing on the centre line makes the building look symmetrical behind the statue.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the clock tower up with the central vertical line. Put the statue low in the frame and the tower above it. If the building is cut off, walk a few steps back along the street rather than tilting the phone up. For an alternative, try Hồ Chí Minh Square for a low, upward-angled shot of the statue with the clock tower rising behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale walls do not turn white. In the evening, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a rail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon for softer light on the facade. In the evening, once the building is illuminated, is the other good time.

text.access_note: The boulevard in front is a public street. The building is a working government office and its interior is generally closed, but arrangements may vary: public opening may be offered on the last weekend of each month, and tours may need registration. Check the current opening arrangements before you go if you hope to see inside.

name: Mariamman Temple, Ho Chi Minh City
label: Mariamman Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Đường Trương Định' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Đường Trương Định nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/187949849: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sri Mariamman Temple' (55 m across).
notes: Colourful Hindu temple with a sculpted gopuram tower.

text.description:
Mariamman Temple is a small, colourful Hindu temple in the middle of District 1, dedicated to the goddess Mariamman. It was built in the late 19th century by the Nagarathar, a trading community from Tamil Nadu in India. Its red-and-orange frontage looks quite different from the glass towers and shopfronts around it, and that contrast is the main reason it photographs well.

The tall, tiered gopuram (the decorated tower) above the main entrance is the star of the picture. It is about 12 m high and carries a number of statues. Inside, statues of Mariamman and other deities line the outer walls and hallways, which gives you close-up details if you go in.

For a phone, the street view is a one-shot job: stand square to the entrance, keep your gridlines on so the tower stays upright, and let the gopuram rise above the doorway. If you want a quieter, closer view of the frontage and its decoration, Chùa Bà Ấn's courtyard is a good second position. Be polite with other visitors: this is a working place of worship, so ask before photographing people who are praying, and keep flash off.
text.geographic_location: In District 1 of Ho Chi Minh City, on Trương Định street at number 45.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The address is 45 Trương Định street, in District 1. Once there, cross to the opposite side of the street from the main entrance and stand. The temple is about 26 m to the south-west of it, a short walk if you want to go over to the entrance. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the facade. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if traffic or the narrow pavement stops you stepping back. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the statues on the gopuram.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Đường Trương Định (opposite side of the street from the main entrance). The red-and-orange facade with the tall multi-tiered gopuram above the main entrance, framed against the surrounding city street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Stand square to the entrance and use the gridlines to keep the gopuram vertical. Leave a little space above the tower, and let the street and neighbouring buildings show at the edges so the contrast with the city is part of the picture. For a closer, quieter view of the frontage and its decoration, try the courtyard at Chùa Bà Ấn as an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the red and orange stay rich and the sky is not washed out. Wait for a gap in the passing scooters before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and lighter traffic, though the street view works at any daylight hour.

text.access_note: Admission is free and photography is generally allowed, but it is a place of worship, so dress modestly, keep flash off, ask permission near worshippers and sacred areas, and avoid drones.

name: Bùi Viện Street
label: Bui Vien Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bùi Viện' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Bùi Viện and Trần Hưng Đạo (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q11334291: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Backpacker street, lively with neon at night.

text.description:
Bùi Viện Street is a short street in the Bến Thành area, known as Ho Chi Minh City's nightlife street. It is lined with small bars and beer gardens, and most visitors come after dark. That is also when it photographs best, because the neon signs, the lit-up shopfronts and the crowd all give you colour and movement in one frame.

The street starts at a Y-junction with Trần Hưng Đạo Boulevard in the east and runs west to a T-junction with Cống Quỳnh street. The area around it, with Đề Thám, Phạm Ngũ Lão and Đỗ Quang Đẩu, is nicknamed the 'Backpacker Quarter'. The street took its present name in 1955, after the 19th-century reformer and diplomat Bùi Viện. In 2017 it was rebuilt as a walking street, and it opened on 20 August 2017 as the city's second pedestrian street, after Nguyễn Huệ Boulevard.

For the best-known shot, stand at the east entrance gate, where the street meets Trần Hưng Đạo Boulevard. Look west under the entrance arch and along the street into the neon-lit crowd. Hold the phone at eye level or slightly lower so the arch frames the scene. If you want a second view, the bar balconies give a high, overhead look down the street, with the light canopy above the crowd. Vehicles still pass through at times, so keep clear of the carriageway while you shoot.
text.geographic_location: Bùi Viện Street is in the Bến Thành area of central Ho Chi Minh City. Its east end meets Trần Hưng Đạo Boulevard, next to the Trần Hưng Đạo – Nguyễn Thái Học crossroads.
text.directions_text: Start from the Bến Thành area and take a taxi or hired scooter to the Trần Hưng Đạo Boulevard end of Bùi Viện Street, by the Trần Hưng Đạo – Nguyễn Thái Học crossroads. From there, the subject point on the map is about 143 m to the north-east. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the arch and the street ahead. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is crowded and you cannot step back. Use 2x if you want to pick out the signs and bring the far end of the street closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Bùi Viện and Trần Hưng Đạo (east entrance gate, where the street meets Trần Hưng Đạo Boulevard). The entrance arch with the street stretching west into the neon-lit crowd, shot at eye level or slightly low.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone at eye level or slightly low, with the arch around the top of the frame, and turn on the gridlines to keep the verticals straight. Let the street lead the eye away from you. For a different view, a bar balcony gives a high shot down the whole street; choose a bar on site, and use the default lens (1x) with the phone held steady against the railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the scene to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the neon keeps its colour instead of turning white. Night mode helps in the dark side streets, but ask people to stay still for a moment, or you will get blur. Live Photos can catch the movement of the crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the signs and lights are on and the street is busy. The street is closed to vehicles on Saturday and Sunday evenings from 7 pm, so those evenings are the easiest for walking and framing. Check locally, as arrangements can change.

text.access_note: Open public street, free to walk. Vehicles still pass at times, so stay clear of the carriageway; check the official site before you go for current walking-street arrangements.
claims_not_in_sources: The neon signs and street lighting are lit from dusk onwards, so the street looks best after dark.
The street is usually busiest in the late evening.
A bar balcony viewpoint may expect you to buy something; this varies by venue.
Phones should be held securely in a crowded street (general caution).
Night mode needs the subject to stay still for a moment to avoid blur (general phone behaviour).

name: Rex Hotel
label: Rex Hotel
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Nguyễn Huệ – Lê Thánh Tôn corner' (1 web pages); placed at crossing of Nguyễn Huệ and Lê Thánh Tôn (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q7319215: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Famous hotel with a rooftop bar and crown sign.

text.description:
The Rex Hotel is one of central Saigon's best-known buildings, and it photographs well because it sits right on a busy street corner, so you can see its whole shape at once. It stands at the corner of Lê Lợi Boulevard and Nguyễn Huệ Boulevard in District 1. It is a six-storey building with 286 rooms. The 1927 building began as a two-storey car showroom and garage for a French businessman, and it displayed Citroën and other European cars. It later became a hotel. During the Vietnam War it hosted the daily US military press briefings that journalists nicknamed "The Five O'Clock Follies", and its rooftop bar was a well-known meeting place for officials and war correspondents. It has carried the Rex name again since 1986.

From there the hotel's corner façade and its signage sit against the street junction. Stand back a little and frame the full building rather than just the sign. Pedestrians and scooters passing through the foreground give the picture a sense of the city. If you want a second angle, Nguyễn Huệ Walking Street shows the frontage down the wide pedestrian boulevard, and Ho Chi Minh City Hall gives a more distant view of the hotel across the civic grounds.
text.geographic_location: In District 1, the central district of Ho Chi Minh City, on the corner of Lê Lợi Boulevard and Nguyễn Huệ Boulevard. Lê Thánh Tôn Street also runs along the building.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so start from central District 1 and go to the Nguyễn Huệ and Lê Lợi boulevards, by taxi or hired scooter if you are coming from further away. From there the hotel is to the south-east, about 1 minute on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the building. If the whole façade will not fit, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the signage or the upper floors.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Nguyễn Huệ and Lê Thánh Tôn (corner facing the hotel's frontage). The hotel's corner façade and signage framed against the street junction, the classic full-building angle. Face south-east towards the hotel's corner frontage. Check the exact corner on the map before you set off.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the building's vertical edges up with them, so the walls do not lean. Leave some street in the foreground. If you want a second view, Nguyễn Huệ Walking Street shows the frontage down the boulevard with passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the sign to set exposure, then slide the exposure control down slightly so the signage does not wash out. In the evening, use night mode and hold your phone against something steady, such as a wall or a post.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually calmer for a clear view of the building. After dark, the lit-up signage gives a different mood, but the junction is busy then.

text.access_note: The façade can be photographed from the public street, but the hotel and its arcade are commercial premises, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: Xá Lợi Pagoda
label: Xa Loi Pagoda
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bà Huyện Thanh Quan' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Bà Huyện Thanh Quan nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1005868: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Buddhist pagoda with a tall bell tower.

text.description:
Xá Lợi Pagoda is the largest pagoda in Ho Chi Minh City. It sits in District 3 on a plot of about 5,000 square metres. Building began in 1956 and the pagoda opened in 1958, to house a sample of relics of the Buddha, which gives it its name. Later, in 1963, it became known as one of the Buddhist pagodas raided during the protests of that year. It is still a working place of worship, so keep your visit quiet and respectful.

For a phone photo, the bell tower is the easiest subject. It is seven storeys tall and stands beside the main gate, with the pagoda entrance behind it. From the pavement outside you get a straight-on view of tower, gate and entrance together, which is a tidy, balanced shot. A gated fence separates the grounds from the street, and just inside it is a popular Chinese-style statue of Quan Âm, which makes a good second picture. Another garden view has the statue framed with the bell tower, library and main building behind it.

The garden and gates can be photographed from outside without fuss. Ask permission before photographing the interior or any worshippers. Opening times can change, so check before you go.
text.geographic_location: Xá Lợi Pagoda is in District 3 of Ho Chi Minh City, on the street Bà Huyện Thanh Quan. Its main gate and bell tower face the pavement.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, tram or similar stops to start from, so go by taxi or hired scooter to Xá Lợi Pagoda in District 3 and ask to be dropped on Bà Huyện Thanh Quan, outside the main gate. Look for the tall bell tower beside the gate. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the straight-on view of the bell tower, gate and entrance. If the pavement is too narrow to fit the whole tower, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Use 2x telephoto to pick out the entrance behind the tower, or the Quan Âm statue, from the same spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Bà Huyện Thanh Quan (on the pavement in front of the main gate). The seven-storey bell tower beside the main gate, with the pagoda entrance behind it. The pagoda is just to the south-west of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the bell tower on one of the vertical lines, with the entrance in the rest of the frame. Keep the phone level, or the tower will lean. If you want a different picture, the garden statue of Guanyin framed with the bell tower, library and main building makes a good alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the details of the tower do not wash out. Take a second shot at 0.5x as a safety option.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon is usually a good choice, as the light tends to be softer. Check the pagoda's opening times first.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship; the gate and garden can be photographed from outside, but check opening times before you go, and ask permission before photographing inside or any worshippers.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late-afternoon light is usually softer.
Visitors to a pagoda are generally expected to dress modestly and keep quiet.
A phone held level avoids a leaning-tower effect, and the ultra-wide lens helps in a narrow pavement space.

name: Saigon Central Mosque
label: Saigon Central Mosque
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Đông Du' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Đông Du nearest the subject (our map tiles).

notes: Blue-and-white mosque built in 1935.

text.description: Saigon Central Mosque is a small, white and blue place of worship on a busy city street, and that is what makes it work as a photograph. The mosque was completed in 1935, after building began on 21 December 1934. It was first known as the India Jamia Muslim Mosque, and the project was led by JM Mohamed Ismael, who headed the British Indian Muslim community. The building is described as Roman in style and has four minarets. In October 1954 Jawaharlal Nehru and Indira Gandhi visited it during Nehru's trip to Vietnam. The best-value photo is the one that shows how small the mosque is next to the modern city. From Đông Du, look towards the Sheraton and the high-rise towers behind the mosque. That makes a quieter, more contextual picture than a straight-on facade shot. If you want the classic view instead, stand on the street in front of the entrance and frame the white and blue facade with its minarets. Traffic is constant, so wait for a gap before you step back to compose. Photograph from outside. Public access can vary, so check on the day and ask before taking any pictures inside.
text.geographic_location: The mosque stands on Đông Du street in central Ho Chi Minh City, close to the Sheraton hotel and the city towers.
text.directions_text: No station is listed nearby, so go by taxi or hired scooter to Đông Du street in central Ho Chi Minh City, near the Sheraton. Look for the white and blue mosque on the street frontage. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the mosque and the towers in one frame. Try 2x if your phone has it, as it makes the towers behind look closer to the mosque. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are tight against the street, and keep the phone level so the minarets do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Đông Du (stretch in front of the mosque, looking toward the Sheraton and the city towers). The mosque's exterior with high-rise hotels behind it, showing the contrast between the small mosque and the surrounding city. From there the mosque is to the north-west of you, with the Sheraton and the city towers rising behind it, which shows the small mosque against the big city.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the mosque on the lower third, with the towers filling the sky above it. Wait for a gap in the traffic so the street does not cut across the foreground. For a second, closer picture, move to the street in front of the entrance and frame the white and blue facade with its minarets.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the mosque to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the white walls keep their detail rather than turning pale. Take a few frames, as people and vehicles keep passing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the white walls and less glare. Go whenever the street is quietest.

text.access_note: This is a place of worship and public access can vary, so check on the day or ask locally before you go, photograph from the street, and ask before shooting inside.
